passages.happening:
‘These are the words of Nehemiah son of Hacaliah: In the month of Chislev, in the twentieth year, while I was in the citadel of Susa’ (verse 1), his brother Hanani arrives with some men from Judah. Nehemiah asks them about the Jews who had survived the exile, and about Jerusalem.

They answer, “The remnant who survived the exile are there in the province, in great trouble and disgrace. The wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates are burned with fire” (verse 3).

‘When I heard these words, I sat down and wept. I mourned for days, fasting and praying before the God of heaven’ (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
The twentieth year is the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes I (2:1), and Chislev, in November and December, falls late in 446 BC. Nearly a century had passed since the first exiles came home under Cyrus, and about thirteen years since Ezra arrived, on the traditional dating. The temple stood. The city around it was still defenseless and mostly empty.

Susa, in what is now southwestern Iran, was one of the royal capitals of the Persian empire, where the kings often spent the winter. Archaeologists have dug up the great palace Darius I built there. The citadel was its fortified royal quarter. The book of Esther is set in the same city.

The broken wall and burned gates could be the old damage from the Babylonian destruction of 587 or 586 BC, or newer damage after the king's order stopped the rebuilding (Ezra 4:23). Many scholars favor the second, because the news came to Nehemiah as a fresh shock.

To a Jew far away, the ruin of Jerusalem was not just bad news from a distant province. It was the city God had chosen for his name, where Nehemiah's fathers were buried. A city without walls was open to raids and could not be a safe home or a place of honor. Its disgrace touched the honor of Israel's God.

Nehemiah's response follows the old patterns of mourning and prayer: he sits, weeps, fasts for days, and prays. The book begins not with action but with grief.
passages.later:
Psalm 137 gives voice to the same love of a ruined city from far away: ‘If I forget you, O Jerusalem, may my right hand cease to function’ (Psalm 137:5).

The order the walls had stood under is told in Ezra: officials went to Jerusalem ‘and forcibly stopped them’ (Ezra 4:23).
passages.hard:
Chapter 1 sets this news in Chislev of the twentieth year, and chapter 2 sets Nehemiah's talk with the king in Nisan of the same twentieth year. Nisan is the first month of the usual year, so how can it come after Chislev?

Scholars explain it in different ways. Nehemiah may have counted the king's years from the anniversary of his accession, or from a year that began in the autumn. Or the text of 1:1 may first have read the nineteenth year. None of the explanations changes the story: the news came in the winter, and Nehemiah waited about four months before he spoke to the king.
passages.asks: Nehemiah wept over a city he had perhaps never seen. Ask what news about God's people moves you to grief, and what leaves you untouched. And ask whether your grief turns to prayer, as his did, before it turns to anything else.

passages.happening:
Nehemiah prays. “O LORD, God of heaven, the great and awesome God who keeps His covenant of loving devotion with those who love Him and keep His commandments” (verse 5), let Your ears hear the prayer ‘that I, Your servant, now pray before You day and night’ (verse 6).

He confesses. ‘I confess the sins that we Israelites have committed against You. Both I and my father’s house have sinned’ (verse 6). They have not kept the commandments given through Moses (verse 7).

Then he reminds God of his own word. “Remember, I pray, the word that You commanded Your servant Moses” (verse 8): if Israel was unfaithful, God would scatter them among the nations, but if they returned to him, ‘then even if your exiles have been banished to the farthest horizon, I will gather them from there’ (verse 9).

And he ends with a request: “Give Your servant success this day, I pray, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man” (verse 11). Only then does the reader learn who he is: ‘At that time I was the cupbearer to the king’ (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The prayer is built from Scripture. Its opening praise of the God who keeps his covenant of loving devotion comes from Deuteronomy, and Daniel's prayer opens the same way. Its confession uses the language of the law's warnings. Its appeal joins the warning of scattering to the promise of gathering from the farthest horizon, to the place God had chosen for his name.

It moves in a clear order: praise, confession, God's own promise, and then a specific request. And it does not blame earlier generations alone. Nehemiah says that he and his own family have sinned.

Remember, zakar, does not suggest that God has forgotten. It is a covenant plea, asking God to act on what he said. The word becomes the book's signature: Nehemiah will ask God again and again to remember him.

The last verse turns suddenly from the God of heaven to ‘this man’, the king. A cupbearer served the king his wine and often tasted it first to guard against poison. The post needed complete trust and gave daily access to the king, so Nehemiah was one of the few people in the empire who could speak to him directly. His prayer for success is a prayer for the conversation he is about to risk.
passages.later:
Nehemiah's first words echo the law: ‘the faithful God who keeps His covenant of loving devotion for a thousand generations of those who love Him and keep His commandments’ (Deuteronomy 7:9). The promise he holds God to is Moses' own: ‘Even if you have been banished to the farthest horizon, He will gather you and return you from there’ (Deuteronomy 30:4).

Daniel began his prayer of confession the same way: “O, Lord, the great and awesome God, who keeps His covenant of loving devotion to those who love Him and keep His commandments” (Daniel 9:4).

And the office of cupbearer is an old one in the Bible. Joseph's fellow prisoner was Pharaoh's chief cupbearer, who ‘once again placed the cup in Pharaoh’s hand’ (Genesis 40:21).
passages.asks: Nehemiah prayed for days before he asked for anything, and when he asked, he asked for something specific. Ask whether your prayers ever reach that point, or stay vague. And ask what promise of God you could pray back to him, as Nehemiah did.
